text: Description and Explanation This second edition of Regional Model Life Tables and Stable Populations incorporates an extension in range of the original tables, an extension that will be particularly useful in applications to populations with low mortality.

Description and Explanation 
This second edition of Regional Model Life Tables and Stable Populations 
incorporates an extension in range of the original tables, an extension 
that will be particularly useful in applications to populations with low 
mortality.

text: JOHN GRAUNT, 1662 Life tables provide a succinct description of what is the most prominent aspect of the state of human mortality: they show the varying chances of dying as a function of age.

chapter_title: Chapter 3. The method of calculation was to deterÂ­
Chapter 3. The method of calculation was to deterÂ­
text: A regression of a particular functional form (linear, quadratic, logarithmic, etc.) often fits the data better over some parts of the range of observations than others, and often represents the data poorly at extremes, and may in particular provide an implauÂ­ sible extension or extrapolation of relationships beyond the range of observations.

beyond the range of observations.

text: "Least-squares" regression equations of any given functional form establish two relations between any pair of variables, as each is considered the indeÂ­ pendent variable, and the other dependent.

text: In an estimation of one variable from a known value of another, the use of one variable as dependent and the other as independent is clearly appropriate and there is a logical reason for employing one regression rather than the other.

text: We would suggest utilizing the "West" family in the usual circumstances of underdeveloped countries where there is no reliable guide to the age pattern of mortality that prevails.
text_raw:
We would suggest utilizing the "West" family in the 
usual circumstances of underdeveloped countries 
where there is no reliable guide to the age pattern of 
mortality that prevails.

text: The other families can be moderately useful in these circumstances to illustrate the variability in estimates that arises from assuming well-established age patterns of mortality other than the pattern underlying the "West" tables.
text_raw:
The other families can be 
moderately useful in these circumstances to illustrate 
the variability in estimates that arises from assuming 
well-established age patterns of mortality other than 
the pattern underlying the "West" tables.

text: We must concede that this use of the four families is far from satisfactory, because there is no strong reason for supposing that the age patterns of mortality exhibited in these four families covers anything like the full range of variability in age patterns in populations under different circumstances.
text_raw:
We must 
concede that this use of the four families is far from 
satisfactory, because there is no strong reason for 
supposing that the age patterns of mortality exhibited 
in these four families covers anything like the full 
range of variability in age patterns in populations 
under different circumstances.

text: At the same time, we feel that the age patterns of mortality exhibited in life tables from underdeveloped areas are usually quite untrustworthy because of defects in the underlying data.
text_raw:
At the same time, we 
feel that the age patterns of mortality exhibited in life 
tables from underdeveloped areas are usually quite 
untrustworthy because of defects in the underlying 
data.

text: The question of what is the pattern of mortality in a population of an underdeveloped area is essenÂ­ tially unresolvable, because there exists no way to deÂ­ termine exactly the age of an illiterate person who does not know it himself, and a fortiori of a deceased person who did not know his own age at the time of death.

MODEL STABLE POPULATIONS 
TABULATION OF STABLE POPULATIONS 
The large number of parameters tabulated for each 
stable population, and the large number of age distriÂ­
butions included in this volume are designed to make 
the tables as widely useful as possible, given the limiÂ­

text: The scheme of tabulation is designed with two conÂ­ siderations in mind:
text_raw:
The scheme of tabulation is designed with two conÂ­
siderations in mind:

text: (a) to provide stable age distribuÂ­ tions for the full range of mortality and fertility levels likely to be relevant either in fitting the tables to obÂ­ served data, or in analyzing the hypothetical conseÂ­ quences of fertility and mortality schedules; and (b) to tabulate values at small enough intervals so that linear interpolation is sufficiently exact.

text: MULTIPLE INTERPOLATION IN THE STABLE AGE DISTRIBUTION TABLES In using these tables, it is essential to recall that each stable age distribution is the consequence of a mortalÂ­ ity schedule and a growth rate, that there are a variety of parameters (birth rate, death rate, mean age) that are implied by each distribution, and that all that is implied about fertility in any age distribution is that the schedule must be one of many possibilities having an appropriate combination of GRR and m.
text_raw:
MULTIPLE INTERPOLATION IN THE STABLE AGE 
DISTRIBUTION TABLES 
In using these tables, it is essential to recall that each 
stable age distribution is the consequence of a mortalÂ­
ity schedule and a growth rate, that there are a variety 
of parameters (birth rate, death rate, mean age) that 
are implied by each distribution, and that all that is 
implied about fertility in any age distribution is that 
the schedule must be one of many possibilities having 
an appropriate combination of GRR and m.

text: In the universe of stable age distributions assoÂ­ ciated with any one of the four families of model life tables, it is possible to locate a unique stable populaÂ­ tion from knowledge of two nonredundant parameÂ­ ters, such as the birth rate and el, the rate of increase and el, the proportion under 20 and the rate of inÂ­ crease, or the average age and the death rate.
text_raw:
In the universe of stable age distributions assoÂ­
ciated with any one of the four families of model life 
tables, it is possible to locate a unique stable populaÂ­
tion from knowledge of two nonredundant parameÂ­
ters, such as the birth rate and el, the rate of increase 
and el, the proportion under 20 and the rate of inÂ­
crease, or the average age and the death rate.

text: HowÂ­ ever, it must be borne in mind that measures of total fertility (such as the GRR) do not constitute in themÂ­ selves an adequate parameter in identifying a unique stable population, but must be supplemented by the mean age of the fertility schedule, and by some other variable as well.
